replacements.old_heading: The River That Teaches You to Read Movement
replacements.old_body: On February 2, World Wetlands Day recalls the convention adopted at Ramsar in 1971. In videogames, few rivers are as readable as Frogger's. Konami's 1981 arcade game divides the screen into two systems of movement: a road crossed by avoiding traffic, and a river that cannot be swum but must be traversed by using logs, turtles and other moving bodies. It is an extreme simplification rather than an ecological simulation, and that is precisely why it shows how an environment can become a rule. The river is not scenery: it determines timing, trajectories, risks and footholds. Frogger builds a miniature atlas of relationships between space, rhythm and survival.
replacements.heading: Crossing the road and river
replacements.body: Frogger is a 1981 action video game developed by Konami and published by Sega for arcades. It was released in North America by Sega/Gremlin. The object of the game is to direct five frogs to their homes by dodging traffic on a busy road, then crossing a river by jumping on floating logs, turtles, and alligators.

replacements.old_heading: Horror Finds a Rhythm to Learn
replacements.old_body: On September 26, 1986, Konami released Akumajō Dracula in Japan for the Famicom Disk System, the work that would originate the series known internationally as Castlevania. It is important to separate this version from the later NES cartridge adaptation, released in North America in 1987 and in Europe afterward. In the original game, Simon Belmont advances through a castle organized as a sequence of short, severe trials, where jumping, whip attacks and sub-weapons require preparation more than improvisation. The apparent rigidity of movement is part of the risk: every command occupies time and space. Monsters drawn from Western horror iconography, Gothic settings and a strong sonic identity turn a linear action structure into an immediately recognizable repertoire destined to be reworked for decades.
replacements.heading: Simon Belmont enters Dracula's castle
replacements.body: Castlevania, known in Japan as Akumajō Dracula, is a 1986 platform game developed and published by Konami. Players control Simon Belmont, descendant of a legendary vampire hunter, who enters the castle of Count Dracula to destroy him when he suddenly reappears 100 years after Simon's ancestor vanquished him.

replacements.old_heading: Before Sonic, SEGA Was Looking for Its Hero
replacements.old_body: On November 2, 1986, for this editorial exception in the calendar, Alex Kidd in Miracle World is associated with its Japanese debut on the Sega Mark III. Official SEGA documentation actually records November 1, 1986, a discrepancy preserved in the verification note. The game was created while SEGA was looking for an action game capable of distinguishing the Mark III from the success of Super Mario Bros.: the project began from an idea closer to an action adventure and was rewritten around a protagonist who fights with his fists, breaks blocks, swims and uses vehicles. Miracle World alternates platforming, exploration, purchasable items and rock-paper-scissors duels, turning each area into a small variation on the rules. Alex Kidd thus became one of the symbolic characters of pre-Sonic SEGA and a valuable record of the company's search for identity in the 8-bit era.
replacements.heading: A platform adventure for the Master System
replacements.body: Alex Kidd in Miracle World is a platform game developed and published by Sega for the Master System. The player must finish levels and overcome obstacles and puzzles in both scrolling and single-screen environments. Throughout the 17 stages, Alex faces many monsters and the three henchmen of Janken the Great, before facing Janken himself.
